technical-data.invention-title: BANDSAW APPARATUS AND METHOD OF OPERATION
SCIE A RUBAN ET SON PROCEDE D'ACTIONNEMENT

abstract.p: A method of operating a bandsaw is disclosed. By stopping a bandsaw between saw cuts it is possible to reduce fatigue in wide bandsaw blades significantly. This, and a gullet (3.04) stress reduction strategy have resulted in a sixty three percent increase in bandsaw blade thickness (1.04, 2.02) for a given wheel diameter (2.05) while maintaining high strain. To achieve this it is necessary to redesign the bandsaw. To that end, descriptions of three bandsaw drive systems are described along with the required band wheel modifications.

L'invention concerne un procédé d'actionnement d'une scie à ruban. En arrêtant une scie à ruban entre des traits de scie, il est possible de réduire considérablement l'usure d'une lame épaisse de scie à ruban. Ce procédé, ainsi qu'une technique de réduction de la contrainte du creux de la dent (3.04) ont permis d'augmenter de 63 % l'épaisseur (1.04, 2.02) de la lame de la scie à ruban pour un diamètre (2.05) de volant donné tout en maintenant une tension élevée. Pour obtenir ce résultat, il est nécessaire de remanier la scie à ruban. A cette fin, l'invention contient la description de trois systèmes de commande de scie à ruban, ainsi que des modifications nécessaires du volant de scie.

description.p: Bandsaw Apparatus and Method of Operation
Background of the invention Field of the invention
This invention relates to bandsaws and more particularly is directed towards reducing the size of band wheels for a given application via an improved method of operation
Description of the prior art

Bandsaws come in a huge variety of sizes. Blade widths 3.03 vary from a few millimetres to 0 4 metres or more. Band wheel diameters 2.05 vary from 0.4 metres to 3 metres or more in diameter. Power requirements vary from less than 1 kilowatt to in excess of 150 kilowatts. One thing that all bandsaws have in common is the blades fatigue as a consequence of spinning around the band wheels 2.01 Tins can lead to cracking m the saw gullets 3.04 and subsequent blade failure
The factors that result in an increased level of fatigue m bandsaw blades 1.01 and 3.01 and 2.07 are listed below. 1 : Thicker gauge of blade (t) 1.04 and 2.02 for a given band wheel diameter
2: Higher bandsaw blade strain
3: Running bandsaw blade too long
4: Misalignment of the band wheels
5: Poorly machined band wheels 6: Misalignment of the saw guides 2.06 and 4.09
7: Saw guides that are not flat
8: Misalignment of the saw head relative to the cutting direction
9: Poor tracking of bandsaw blade on band wheel
10: Incorrect bandsaw blade tension 11 : Uneven grinding of bandsaw blade
12: Stress concentranon points in bottom of saw gullet
13- Attempting to cut too fast
14: Cutting with a blunt blade
15: Excessive hook angle 3.02 16 Vibration m bandsaw or saw blade

All these factors are extremely important. All but 1. 2, 3 and 12 will cause poor cutting. Note that 3 and 14 are not the same. A bandsaw blade may have spent a lot of time spinning and not cutting and/or cutting a soft timber that blunts the saw at a slower rate. Factors 1 and 2 actually improve performance, a thicker more stable blade permits a deeper gullet, which can hold more sawdust, allowing faster cutting. As a rule saw gullet depth and consequently gullet volume increase in propoπion to the saw gauge. .All the literature that I am aware of limits the thickness of the bandsaw blade to roughly 1/1000 of the diameter of the band wheel, a ratio (R) of 0 001 Traditionally. strain was set in proportion to the cross sectional area of the saw blade (W.t). Modern strain theory has turned this on its head. The relationship is now inverted This is the result of attempts to quannfy the amount of strain due to the blade bending around the
band wheel Thus modern thin kerf high strain saws came into being Reducing die blade thickness to wheel diameter ratio to R = 0 000583 allowed in excess of a ten fold increase in cross sectional area blade strain The ceiling on R remamed at 0 001 Although I know of some operators pushing that ceiling by 10% (R = 0 0011 ) Inside 5 this range there are operators who are having problems with cracking and there are those that aren't

Machines running narrow blades (under 50mm wide and occasionally as wide as 75mm) present a different set of problems Narrow blades may significantly exceed the thickness test shown above because they are cheap and consequently may be

10 considered disposable Manufacturers of narrow bladed machines talk terms of 'blade flex life" This is an admission that blades have a limited life in their application It is uncommon to find these blades being sharpened more than twenty times in their life Nor will they run for anywhere near as long between sharpenings Typically in Australia, cutting hardwood, these blades will fail after one days cutting i 5 Consequently they aren t exposed to the same level of fatigue as a wide band, which may be sharpened a hundred nines or more and run for a hundred days duπng its life The cost of these narrow blades are typically less than 10% of the cost of blades for a bandsaw running wide blades Narrow blades are mass produced, smaller and have teeth that are set side to side, whereas wide blades are custom built and have swaged. 0 stellite or tungsten teeth

Cutting rates and accuracy are influenced by the cross section area of the saw gullet 3.04 The wider the saw cut the larger the gullet must be If the gullet area is too small sawdust may overflow in the cut causing heatmg and wandering of the saw blade The solution to this is to slow the cutting rate This results in a finer sawdust and 5 premature blunting of the blade The finer sawdust falls out of the gullet m the cut and may also interfere with saw tracking The gullet depth is limited by the thickness of the saw blade Too deep a gullet and the tooth will be weakened

Disposable narrow blades are not a solution to the problem of fatigue in wide bandsaw blades The blades do not have the stability to cut as wide or as fast as wide 0 blades Nor will they cut Australian hardwoods as successfully (if at all) Narrow bladed bandsaw mills have become popular through lower capital cost

Narrow bladed mobile bandsaws have previously been described with brake and clutch systems to stop the blade These are small machines The wheels at a guess may weigh less than 20kg All have been developed for safety not performance Their 5 aim is to bπng the blade to a stop m a matter of seconds not minutes

In LiS patent number 4559858 a brake and clutch svstem is descπbed The only suggested benefit is safety This patent doesn t refer to narrow bladed machines however the onlv manifestations have been narrow bladed machines Further more a reference ' 14 hp petrol motor should for mobile applications" indicates the rntennon 0 is for low Dower applications At first glance it would appear that the brake and clutch descπption gives broad coverage .An earlier L S patent 4275632 describes a clutch to facilitate stopping the saw This effectively narrows the scope of US patent 4559858 to the specific lavout described

Another proposal. LS patent number 3954037 suggested that driving the bandsaw 5 blade with a linear electric motor here the blade becomes the armature, would allow
wheel size to be reduced because blade gπp on the band wheel becomes less important This fails to recognize the importance of fatigue in wide bandsaw blades It would be unpractical to reduce wheel size without a fatigue reduction strategy Tins aside, I have never found wheel gπp to be a problem with bandsaws This is certainly not an issue with high strain svstems

We are left with a situation where cutting dense hardwood, or cutting faster or wider, with a high level of performance, can only be accomplished with a wider, heavier gauge blade Tins requires a lareer oand wheel This would appear to be the mitins factor in bandsaw performance Brief description of the drawings

This mvention features a method of operating a wide bladed bandsaw that has developed from a bandsaw blade fatigue reduction strategy The result of which is that the limiting factor m bandsaw operation, the ratio of bandsaw blade thickness to band wheel diameter (R) has been significantly increased

The problem of stress concentrations in the gullet of the bandsaw blade is further complicated by the effect of blade spm time on accumulated fatigue in bandsaw blades An analysis of the time duπng which the blade is spinnmg that is spent cutting is useful Tins will be shown as a percentage (T)

Most bandsaws at least have down time returning to the start position and repositioning for the next cut (T=50%) If left runnmg duπng log turning (T=35%) and log loading (T=20%) down nme mcreases further If the bandsaw is left runnmg continuously, eighty percent of the accumulated fatigue associated with bendmg around the band wheels is generated while not cutting Thus accumulated fatigue is being produced unnecessarily These figures are a rough guide and can vary dramatically m different situations
To limit this fatigue accumulation it is essential that the bandsaw be stopped between cuts To effect this method it is necessary to fundamentally redesign the bandsaw

Conventionally band wheels are built heavily from cast iron for dimensional stability The dπve wheel 4.07 is generally built much more heavily than the dπven wheel 4.11 to produce a flywheel effect Reduced band wheel weight is achieved through a different method of construction It is recommended that the wheels are fabπcated m steel (possibly high grades such as bisalloy) or aluminiu or cast from aluminium If the wheel can be made small enough cast iron may be possible

Bandsaws. designed to facilitate this method of operation, with reduced band wheel diameter and weight, and power plants that permit fast start up and shut down of the bandsaw- are a cπtical part of this invention Three apparatuses are descπbed. one with an automotive dπve train, one is hydrauhcally dπven and the last is powered
an electπc motor with a pneumatically activated clutch and brake- Reducing the diameter and weight of the band wheels for a given application will allow the power required for fast start up of the bandsaw to be better matched to the power required for cuttmg. Trials with 17 gauge blades . major stress concentration Secondly being at the join in the blade and having only happened once it indicates that the crack was caused by a manufactunng fault in the blade Either the weld had been ground to thm or the weld had a fault in it The crack was repaired and did not reoccur Blades on average have been on the saw for between 5 and 20 hours between sharpenmgs. cuttmg both hardwood and softwood until blunt These blades are all stelhte tipped Stel te is a hard mateπal that mamtams a sharp edge longer This works against fatigue reduction as cutting time and therefore blade spin time are increased The loss of the flywheel effect from heavy cast iron band heels appears not to be a problem at all Tπalling of a 16 gauge blade ( a ratio of R = 0 00183. was considered No benefit would have been gamed from this, as the prototype machme now needs a power upgrade Blade speed for cutting widths between 1000mm and 1350mm has been reduced to 22 metres per second (normally 35 m/sec) Nevertheless it is possible to extrapolate from diese figures diat 16 gauge would work for dense, abrasive timbers as blades would only stay on the saw a short time Note that earned to the extreme it mav become necessary to grind the back edge of the saw occasionally to prevent cracking Note that only a lack of power prevents us runmng higher blade speeds for naπow cutting Blade speed is adjusted via the automotive gearbox to facilitate maximum saw chip size Extremely high strain has been mamtained through out this exercise Stram is an important function in bandsaw performance Stram is the amount of force used to push one band wheel away from the other This is done to make the blade as stiff as possible m the cut

What is clear from these results is that we have been able to maintain very high saw stram ( σ . ) m the presence of a bending stram ( σ tιe\ ) apparently never achieved before It is quite clear that we are still operating m a zone well below the ultimate tensile strength of the blade steel 1500 N / mm"

This process clearlv allows at least a 63% mcrease m blade thickness for our application1 The above statement could however read This process clearly allows at least a 38 7% reduction in band wheel diameter for our application1 The resulting lift in cutting performance and quality has been outstanding Other benefits become
apparent Smaller band wheels allow the machine to be brought up to speed quicker for a given power input A given braking system will also stop the bandsaw quicker The capital cost of sawmill plant can be reduced significantly The cost of blades is reduced, as they are shorter Any future advances in steel toughness potentially allowing conventional mills to run thicker gauge blades will benefit our process equally
Description of the preferred embodiments
This description does not set out to descπbe a complete bandsaw Only those parts that relate to the method of operation and the apparatuses designed to effect the method of operation are descπbed
A method of operation of a bandsaw.

A bandsaw of the type compπsing a dπve wheel 4.07 and at least one dπven wheel 4.11, has entrained over it, a bandsaw blade of a width no less than 85mm. where the ratio of bandsaw blade thickness to band wheel diameter exceeds 0 00135 Where future advances m steel toughness, allow bandsaws to run a thicker gauge blade for a given wheel diameter increasing the conventional limit of blade thickness to band wheel diameter from 0 001. then the ratio of blade thickness to band wheel diameter should exceed that new limit by 35 percent

The width of the bandsaw blade is measured from the back edge of the blade to the bottom of the gullet 3.03, and m the case of a double cut bandsaw blade the width should be measured between opposing gullets

The means of dπvmg the bandsaw dπve wheel and the means of braking the saw should facilitate acceleration and deceleration of the band wheels and bandsaw blade at such a rate that will allow the blade to be run up to operating speed in less than 2 5 seconds and stopped agam in the same time frame Reducmg the weight of the band wheels for a given application will allow the power required for fast start up of the bandsaw to be better matched to the power required for cuttmg Quickly stopping the bandsaw is also enabled by the band wheel weight reduction

This method of operation mcludes the following steps A force is applied to the slide mechamsm 4.08 of the dπven bandsaw wheel 4.11. thus applying strain to the bandsaw blade The amount of force that can be applied is 2 x 230 x W x 0 00163 D Newtons where W and D are respectively the width of the saw 2.02 blade and the diameter of the band wheel 2.05

The first step is to position the log or timber for cuttmg. which may include movmg the bandsaw Secondly, it is necessary to engage the means of dπvmg the bandsaw dπve wheel to spm the bandsaw up to operating speed Then, a cut is made through the log or timber Next by usmg the means of braking, the bandsaw may be stopped or slowed To complete the cvcle one of the next two steps occurs
( 1 ) The bandsaw or log or timber is repositioned to effect the next cut (2) The next log or piece of timber is positioned for cutting This may include moving the bandsaw

Where more than one bandsaw blade is cuttmg the timber it may be necessary between cuts to reposition bandsaws relative to each other
These steps are a means of reducing handsaw blade fatigue allowing the blade tn keep cutting until it is no longer sha enough to cut, without placing a time limit on the blade being on the saw Thus deliverm?. a service life tn the blade that allows the blade to be used until sharpening renders it too narrow for efficient use.
The method of operation will still succeed when the ratio of handsaw blade thickness to band wheel diameter is increased to 0.00163 and blade strain is set to σ , = 230 N

The means of reducing bandsaw blade fatigue is aided bv a gullet stress reduction strategy which involves reducing stress concentrations in the gullet 3.04 of the handsaw blade bv firstly ensuring that the bottom of the blade gullet does not have a tight radius and is substantially flat and secondly that the bottom of the gullet has grinding marks removed either bv reaming or some means of polishing.

These apparatuses are significant developments in themselves and can stand alone as inventions. In no way do these apparatuses limit the scope of the method of operation of a bandsaw. They do however illustrate the practical resolution of the problem of fatigue in bandsaw blades. Note that only those parts of the specific embodiment that relate to the process described above are detailed below. This is because the complete machine may assume one of many forms.

A description of the automotive drive train The means of driving the bandsaw comprises an entire automotive drive train including motor 4.01, clutch and gearbox 4.02, tail shaft 4.03, differential 4.04, axle 4-05. brake and hub 4,06 and control means The automotive drive tram may be left in its chassis with the axle housing attached directly to the chassis. Locking or welding the differential centre allows all drive force to be directed to one axle. The gearbox can be shifted to neutral allowing the drive to be disengaged so that the clutch may be released. The control means includes means for controlling engine throttle, clutch, gearbox and brake. The clutch and brake can be controlled by one pedal and the same master cylinder The hub can alternatively he attached to the handsaw drive 5,01 shaft by means of a coupling capable absorbing some degree of misalignment, or the band wheel may be attached directly to the hub

Bv selecting a gear then releasing pressure from the clutch and brake nedal. the clutch is activated and the brake released. Allowing the bandsaw to be accelerated up to operating speed by applying the throttle. Applying pressure to the clutch and brake pedal releases the clutch and applies the brake, thus stopping the bandsaw. A description of the hvdraulic power plant

The power plant supplying power to the hvdraulic pump 6.02 mav be an electric or internal combustion motor. The hydraulic pump via a control valve 6.04 drives the hvdraulic motor 6.03. The hvdraulic motor is mounted directly on the band wheel drive shaft 5.01 or alternatively drives the band wheel drive shaft via a gearbox or other reduction device The hydraulic control valve can he used as a brake to stop the saw. The hydraulic control valve directs hydraulic oil from the pump to the tank while not cutting. The hydraulic control valve may be controlled directly or remotely by the operator, or by computer set works.
Λ. description of the electric motor with pneumatic clutch and brake

An electπc motor will overheat if stopped and started as often as this method requires It is necessary to continuously run the electπc motor and release the dπve via a clutch and brake This has already been descπbed in the form of the hydraulic apparatus above Another way of achieving this is with a pneumatic clutch and pneumatically activated brake This allows the dπve to be released and the bandsaw stopped without stoppmg the electπc motor The electπc motor and clutch and brake assembly are mounted directly on the band wheel dπve shaft or alternatively dπve the band wheel dπve shaft via a gearbox or other reduction device The pneumatic control valves may be controlled directly or remotely by the operator, or by computer set works
